wsj.summary_analysis: Lowe's second-quarter fiscal 2018 report (Aug. 22, 2018) centered on new CEO Marvin Ellison's early moves to close the performance gap with larger rival Home Depot. Lowe's said it would shut down its Orchard Supply Hardware chain, acquired five years earlier out of bankruptcy, with a portfolio review under way for other nonretail investments; the 99 Orchard locations in California, Florida and Oregon are to close by year-end. The company also recruited CVS Health finance chief David Denton as its new CFO. Ellison, who joined in early July after leaving J.C. Penney's CEO post and having previously spent over a decade at Home Depot, described eliminating positions like operating head and customer chief within his first week, and criticized prior leadership for lacking store-level experience ('The person leading our stores team until recently had never worked in a store... I'm not saying that's a prerequisite; what I am saying is, it really helps') and for prioritizing showcasing smart-home products over profitable end-cap placement ('we're more concerned about shouting out to the world that we have smart-home products than we are in saying we're making money'). The article notes Ellison succeeded Robert Niblock, who retired after activist investor D.E. Shaw placed three directors on the board, with Pershing Square's William Ackman also having built a roughly $737 million stake. On earnings, second-quarter sales rose 7.1% to $20.89 billion, with comparable sales up 5.2%, though this still lagged Home Depot's 8.4% sales growth and 8.1% U.S. comparable-sales gain reported the prior week. Net income was $1.52 billion, or $1.86 a share, versus $1.42 billion, or $1.68, a year earlier, including a $230 million Orchard-closure charge; adjusted profit rose to $2.07 a share from $1.57. Lowe's lowered its full-year sales growth forecast to about 4.5% from 5% and comparable-sales guidance to 3% from 3.5%, both tied to the Orchard closure.
wsj.why_moved: The article states Lowe's shares rose 5.8% to $105.52 on the day, the strongest gain among S&P 500 constituents, which it attributes to the combination of stronger-than-expected sales and profit in the quarter alongside Ellison's aggressive early restructuring moves, including the Orchard closure and executive changes, even though sales growth continued to lag Home Depot's. The headline itself frames the share jump as following the stronger earnings and strategic announcements together, without further granular explanation from the article of which element weighed more heavily.
